grantee_partners.q45.value: The proposal development process reinforced several important lessons that I will apply in future GEF project applications. First, it highlighted the importance of building a strong evidence base by clearly demonstrating the environmental problem, its root causes and the expected global environmental benefits. Proposals are much stronger when they are supported by reliable baseline data, stakeholder consultations and alignment with national priorities and GEF focal area strategies. Second, I learned the value of developing a robust Theory of Change that clearly links project activities to outputs, outcomes and long-term impacts, while explicitly identifying assumptions, risks and sustainability measures. Another important lesson is the need to integrate cross-cutting issues, such as gender equality, youth engagement, local communities, climate resilience and knowledge management, throughout the proposal rather than treating them as separate components. Finally, I gained a better understanding of the importance of developing realistic implementation arrangements, a results-based monitoring framework, a sound budget linked to expected outcomes and a sustainability strategy that includes institutional ownership, policy integration and opportunities for co-financing and resource mobilization. These lessons will help me prepare stronger, more strategic and results-oriented GEF proposals that are better aligned with donor requirements while responding effectively to national environmental priorities.

Early clarification of the roles and responsibilities of government agencies, implementing partners and local communities can significantly improve coordination and ownership during implementation.

grantee_partners.q57.value: The resources that contributed most to the progress of our project were a combination of practical guidance, technical expertise and peer learning. In particular, the GEF project proposal development guidelines and templates provided a clear framework for developing a logical, results-oriented and donor-compliant proposal. Training sessions and technical advice from experienced GEF practitioners helped translate the GEF requirements into practical project design. Equally valuable were national policy documents, scientific literature, baseline studies and environmental assessments, which strengthened the evidence base and ensured alignment with national priorities and global environmental objectives. Peer learning and the exchange of experiences with other project developers and practitioners were also highly beneficial, providing practical insights into successful approaches, common challenges and lessons learned during both project design and implementation.

grantee_partners.q45.value: 1. Begin with a documented field assessment, which requires financial support, rather than merely completing a form. This makes the justification verifiable and distinguishes the submission from generic proposals. 2. Align every activity with the GEF results framework. Evaluators look for an explicit logical chain linking the global environmental issue, local activity, and a measurable indicator with a baseline and target. Any activity without an associated indicator weakens the proposal. 3. Involve beneficiaries and technical partners in drafting. Their contributions strengthen the content and build ownership from the outset, avoiding improvised awareness-raising after signature. 4. Build the budget in accordance with donor management rules. 5. Develop a realistic schedule. Account for the time between approval and the first transfer, as well as agricultural seasonality. An overly tight schedule leads to amendments. 6. Match ambition to the size of the funding envelope. With a small grant over twelve months, a focused scope and achievable results are more convincing than a broad promise.

grantee_partners.q45.value: We learned that a strong GEF project proposal must clearly demonstrate the link between the identified community and environmental problems, the proposed activities, expected results, and the GEF SGP priorities. We also learned the importance of developing realistic and detailed budgets that are directly aligned with the activities and expected outputs. Early planning, clear indicators, a strong monitoring and evaluation framework, stakeholder and community consultation, and a clear sustainability plan are also essential. For future proposals, we would begin the preparation process earlier, allow sufficient time for review and revisions, strengthen the use of baseline information and evidence, and seek technical guidance where necessary. We would also ensure that project objectives and expected outcomes are specific, measurable, achievable, and clearly demonstrate how the project will contribute to lasting environmental and community benefits.

grantee_partners.q63.value: Other grantee partners should begin implementation with a clear work plan, realistic budget, strong monitoring system, and well-defined responsibilities for the project team. They should maintain good communication with the SGP country team and technical partners and keep complete documentation of activities, expenditures, procurement, and changes throughout the project. It is also important to build flexibility and risk management into the project from the beginning. Unexpected events, including hurricanes and other climate-related disasters, can significantly affect activities, budgets, timelines, beneficiaries, and project resources. Grantee partners should therefore have contingency plans and understand the procedures for requesting and documenting changes when circumstances require adjustments. Most importantly, they should focus not only on completing activities but on creating sustainable benefits that will continue beyond the SGP funding period.
